newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria's forces kill 40 guerrillas - papers.
newsitem.headline: Algeria's forces kill 40 guerrillas - papers.

text.p: Algeria's security forces have killed 40 Moslem guerrillas, including 12 shot dead after a gun battle of several hours in Algiers, Algerian newspapers said on Thursday.

Residents also reported that security forces were out in force searching for guerrillas ahead of parliamentary elections due on June 5. President Liamine Zeroual has promised maximum security for the ballot.
The 12 guerrillas were killed on Wednesday in an assault on their hideout near a mosque in Beaufraisier district on the northern edge of Algiers, said El Watan newspaper.
It said security forces also killed 25 guerrillas in Sour el Ghozlane, a Moslem rebel stronghold located 90 km (55 miles) south of Algiers. It gave no other details.
The newspaper Liberte said three more rebels were killed on Wednesday in Bab Ali suburb, south of Algiers, after a security force sweep.

News of the latest clashes emerged as the government, in a drive to put anti-Islamist militias under the strict control of regular security forces, issued a law setting tight rules for the militias' operations.

Tens of thousands of anti-Islamists volunteered to join the self-defence groups early in 1995 to guard their villages and small towns from guerrillas blamed by the authorities for massacres in remote hamlets.
But human rights groups have accused some militias, armed by security forces or using their own hunting rifles, of "abuses".

The militia law, outlined in Algerian newspapers on Thursday, bans self-defence group members from storming homes or other buildings unless they receive a call for help from people threatened by Moslem guerrillas.
"The self-defence groups must only be armed by the authorities and must wear obvious uniforms to avoid any mistake or confusion," the law states.
From now on, the defence and interior ministries will work out where and how the groups deploy their forces, it added.
Human rights groups have attacked the Algerian government for what they described as the "dark side" of the pro-government militias and security forces.

The U.S. State Department, in its annual human rights report early this year, said the Algerian government's human rights performance had "improved somewhat" but there were "continued serious human rights abuses".

Algerian newspapers recently widely quoted a report by the government-appointed human rights watchdog, the National Observatory of Human Rights, about unspecified "abuses" by some self-defence group members.
About 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a huge lead.
